published_title: THE VILLAGE THAT COULD NOT SLEEP

story.title: THE VILLAGE THAT COULD NOT SLEEP
story.deck: Fourteen wounded villagers need surgery before the pass closes, every anaesthetic the clinic owns brings the same fever, and the one thing the patients share is not in their blood.
story.shape: Intimate medical emergency in five scenes: a pattern read from the order of the reactions, a prediction written down before the test, one miss that exposes the real source in the clinic itself, and a costly village-wide agreement; the physician, the pilot, the headwoman and the anaesthetist each keep a veto.

scenes.title: Fever
paragraphs: *Nemea clinic, operating room · 14:40*

The third patient began to burn forty seconds after the anaesthetic took. Dr. Corin Hale stopped the drip before the monitor had finished saying so, and the room filled with the sound of everyone breathing in. Bartek Lind, who drove timber trucks and had been dug out of the cab of one that morning, lay rigid under the lights with a temperature climbing a degree every four minutes.

Osvin Pike, seventy, and Tomas Ketter, who tended the upper kilns, had burned the same way an hour before, one after the other. Both had been packed in ice and both had lived, and neither could be put under again. Illuminara had come up the pass with the first relief convoy and had been given a stool in the corner and a promise that she would be told if she was needed. She was needed now. She watched Hale pack the man in ice, and she did not speak until his temperature turned.

**Corin Hale**  
That is the third. Same fever, three different people, and every agent I own does it. It is malignant hyperthermia or something that wears its face. It runs in families, and I have the dantrolene for two bodies, not fourteen.

**Pelagia Rusk**  
These are not families. I have the parish books. Eleven of the fourteen are Nemea people and they came here from three different valleys across a hundred years. Nobody in this clinic is anybody's cousin.

**Corin Hale**  
Then it is bad luck three times, and I do not operate on bad luck.

Dr. Rusk had run the village clinic for thirty years and was wearing the same cardigan she had been wearing when the mountain came down. She laid the list on the counter: fourteen names, four who could wait a night, ten who could not. A ruptured spleen. A pelvis. A girl of nine with a femur through the skin.

**Nell Brandt, on the radio**  
Nemea, Brandt. Pass closes to freezing rain at twenty hundred. I can lift at seventeen and at nineteen, three stretchers a lift. That is six of fourteen. Tell me which six.

**Pelagia Rusk**  
Eight stay behind with an anaesthetic that fevers them.

**Nell Brandt, on the radio**  
Then six, and I will pray for the eight.

Illuminara took the list from the counter and read it as she read a load path, looking for the place where the weight did not go where it should. It took her a long minute. Then she asked Dr. Hale for the three charts, and the times on them.

scenes.title: The Order of the Fevers
paragraphs: *Nemea clinic, ward corridor · 15:05*

She laid the charts side by side on the floor of the corridor, where the light was best. Beside the three reactions she set the two earlier ones from the first-aid post: a hiker named Sana Moreau, splinted with a sedative at noon and perfectly well, and a fourteen-year-old called Ilo Vell, sedated at one o'clock with a fever that had come and gone on its own.

**Illuminara**  
You said it runs in families. Then it would not care where a person slept. Look at it as a gradient and not as a yes and a no. Osvin Pike reacted worst, and he has sat beside an upper-village hearth every winter day for seventy years. Tomas Ketter reacted next. He lives at the kilns. Bartek reacted after him. He has slept two nights at the inn. Ilo reacted least, and he came home from the valley school yesterday evening. Sana reacted not at all. She has been on the ridge for three days and has not been indoors in Nemea once.

**Corin Hale**  
A gradient by hours indoors. That is a coincidence of five.

**Illuminara**  
It is five out of five, and it has a direction. A gene cannot count nights. Something in the houses can. What is in the houses that is not in the valley?

Nobody answered. Down the corridor a woman in a burned shawl, who had been sitting with her injured husband for six hours, lifted her head. This was Marta Vell, who kept the village's resin kilns, and she had not been asked for anything yet.

**Marta Vell**  
Resin. Every house burns it. It has always been so; my grandmother's grandmother burned it. But it is not the old resin, not since the dry autumn.

**Pelagia Rusk**  
What do you mean, not the old resin?

**Marta Vell**  
The upper kilns ran short. We stretched the cakes with bark off the scorched slope, the one that came down today. Dark cake. The houses below the church burn the pale stock still, because they were slow to buy. The kiln houses and the upper houses burn dark.
Illuminara had not known that, and could not have known it, and she said so out loud, so that everyone in the corridor heard what the missing piece had cost to find.

**Illuminara**  
Then I have a prediction, and I would like it written down before anyone is tested. If the dark cake is the cause, the more dark smoke someone has breathed, the slower the enzyme that clears this class of anaesthetic. We can measure that slowness in a drop of plasma in the blood-gas machine. Twelve minutes, no drug given to any patient. Marta, name me the fourteen houses and what each burns.

**Corin Hale**  
And if you are wrong, ten people wait on a hearth superstition.

**Illuminara**  
If I am wrong, the machine says so in twelve minutes, and we have lost less time than your next attempt would cost.
Hale looked at the three charts for a long moment. Then he went to find the plasma tubes.

scenes.title: Twelve Minutes
paragraphs: *Nemea clinic, laboratory corner · 15:20 to 16:15*

She wrote the ranking in the clinic log in ink, with the time, and Rusk signed beneath it as witness. At the bottom: the fourteen names in the order the machine ought to give them, slowest to fastest, built from Marta's list of what each house burned and how long each patient had sat in its smoke. Sana Moreau went last, as the fastest of all.

The machine took two samples at a time. Hale fed it himself with a technician's care and a sceptic's face, and Illuminara stood behind the curtain and did not touch the controls. At minute twelve the first pair settled and the numbers came up. Osvin Pike, slowest by a margin that made the technician swear softly. Bartek Lind, next. The slopes came out in the order she had written. Pair after pair, they came out in that order, and the room went quiet, and the quiet had a texture it had not had at the third fever.

In the fourth pair the order broke. Osvin's grand-niece Ines lived in a pale-stock house below the church. By Marta's list and by Illuminara's ranking she belonged near the fast end. She stood fourth from the slow end.

**Corin Hale**  
There. One in fourteen. Your hearth explains twelve and fumbles the other.

**Illuminara**  
It is wrong, and I am glad it is wrong, because a hearth that explained all fourteen would have been a story. Marta, where did she sit today?

**Marta Vell**  
She sat with Osvin. They carried him here from the slide at nine, and she has not left his bed.
Illuminara did not move for a moment. She had been looking at the houses, and the smoke she had been looking for had been in the room she was standing in.

**Illuminara**  
Dr. Rusk. What does this clinic burn?

**Pelagia Rusk**  
The big stove in the waiting room. The upper kiln sent down a sledge of cake at dawn, to keep the wounded warm. Dark cake. It is the only stove that heats all the beds.
There was a silence in which the hum of the machine was the loudest thing in the building.

**Illuminara**  
Then every patient in this clinic is being dosed more every hour they wait. The longer we argue, the slower the enzyme gets. We are not waiting out a danger. We are feeding it.
On the screen the last pair settled. Sana Moreau, fastest of all, as written. The only fever in the room now was in Hale's face, and he was too honest a physician to hide that it was shame.

scenes.title: The Stove
paragraphs: *Nemea clinic, waiting room · 16:20*

The stove stood at the end of the room like a low black animal, and a dozen faces turned from it to her as she came in. It was nine degrees outside the blanket line. Eight patients lay in shock with their feet toward the heat.

**Pelagia Rusk**  
No. If that goes cold, I lose the spleen and the girl to the chill before any anaesthetic touches them. You have found a poison and want me to put out the only fire.

**Illuminara**  
I want you to change what the fire burns. Marta, how much pale stock is left below the church?

**Marta Vell**  
Forty cakes. It was to last the village until the thaw.

**Illuminara**  
Then I am asking you for the winter, and I will not pretend that is small.

Marta did not answer for the time it takes to count forty cakes against a hundred houses. Behind her a man lying under a coat said something about his own hearth and what it had meant for four hundred years, and she said, without turning, that the hearth had meant it for the living.

**Marta Vell**  
Open the storehouse. But I want it written that the village gave it, and that the dark cake does not go to the lowlands to be sold. It goes in the river.

**Illuminara**  
Written, and I will sign it where the village can read it.

The stove changed its burn within the half hour. Two men from the kilns carried the dark cake out through the side door; Hale opened the high vents; and Illuminara put the second plasma set on the machine at minute forty, as she had said she would, so that nobody could say the plan had been decided before it was tested.
At minute forty the slopes had begun to rise. They rose unevenly, and Osvin Pike, who had breathed the most, had risen almost not at all.

**Corin Hale**  
Told you. He is the one it is in the blood for.

**Illuminara**  
He is also the one who has sat the longest in the smoke. Run him again at seventy. If I am wrong about him, I will be glad to learn it now.
At minute seventy the slope came up, slow and unmistakable. Osvin's was a washout, not a flaw. Hale took the sheet in both hands.

**Corin Hale**  
Then here is what I will do, and not one thing more. Whoever has risen past my line goes under the general. Whoever has not, I block, with the other chemistry, nerve by nerve, and I need each of them or their family to say yes with the numbers in front of them. The block takes me twice as long. I can do ten tonight with Dr. Rusk assisting.

**Pelagia Rusk**  
Ten, and the machine decides the order, not the clock.

**Nell Brandt, on the radio**  
That leaves the two the block cannot reach. The spleen and the girl's leg. I lift at seventeen, two stretchers, and I want it noted that I am not waiting for you to be sure.

**Illuminara**  
I do not need you to wait. I need you to carry them, and the machine will tell Dr. Hale who goes under the general while you are in the air.

Ilo Vell's mother would not sign for the boy's block until Hale put the plasma curve in her hands and showed her where he sat and where the line ran. She read it with a finger. Then she signed, and said that she did not understand a word of it, and that she understood the line.

scenes.title: What the Pass Kept
paragraphs: *Nemea clinic and landing field · 17:00 to 04:10*

The helicopter lifted at 17:02 with the girl of nine and the man with the ruptured spleen, and went up into the beginning of the rain with its lights burning. Brandt radioed from the valley at 17:58 that they were down and handed over. The second lift at nineteen hundred stood on the pad unneeded, and she logged it that way, and told Illuminara afterwards that it was the best use of a flight she had ever made.

Dr. Hale blocked ten that night. He worked from the least recovered to the most, with Rusk's hands beside his, and each time the plasma line had said who should go under and who should not, and each time the family or the patient had said yes to the number. The four who had cleared his line went under the general in the early hours and woke without fevers. The block took twice as long and held, and Osvin Pike was the last man to be wheeled in, at three-forty, with his grand-niece asleep against the wall.
At 04:10 the last suture was in. In the waiting room the stove burned pale cake with its vents open, and nobody was cold, and nobody was feverish.

Illuminara stayed through the rest of the night because there was a log to finish. She wrote the protocol herself, in a plain hand, as Hale would use it and not as she would. A bench test, plasma and substrate, twelve minutes, no drug given. A line below which a patient was blocked, not put under. A pair of readings an hour apart for anyone who breathed smoke of unknown stock, because the slope moved and the machine could tell. Under it she wrote the name of the village that had given the winter, and the date, and Marta Vell signed it where the village could read it.

**Pelagia Rusk**  
What does it cost us? Say the whole of it.

**Illuminara**  
Forty cakes of pale resin, which is the village's heat until the thaw. Dark cake does not burn indoors in Nemea again, and the kilns stand idle until someone finds what in the scorched bark does this. Two of the fourteen face long recoveries far from home. And the line on the sheet is provisional. It comes from fourteen people and one machine, and I would like it checked in a laboratory before anyone trusts it twice.

**Pelagia Rusk**  
Checked. But it was right tonight.

**Illuminara**  
It was wrong once tonight, about Osvin's niece, and that is why it was right about the stove.

Rusk looked down the ward, where the patients slept in the pale light of the new fire. Then she asked Marta Vell to bring in forty cakes from the cold storehouse, and Marta, who had been awake for twenty-two hours, said she would bring them herself.

scenes.title: The Order of the Fevers
paragraphs: *Nemea clinic, ward corridor · 15:05*

She laid the charts side by side on the floor of the corridor, where the light was best. **Pelagia Rusk**  
What do you mean, not the old resin?

**Marta Vell**

scenes.title: Twelve Minutes
paragraphs: *Nemea clinic, laboratory corner · 15:20 to 16:15*

She wrote the ranking in the clinic log in ink, with the time, and Rusk signed beneath it as witness. At the bottom: the fourteen names in the order the machine ought to give them, slowest to fastest, built from Marta's list of what each house burned and how long each patient had sat in its smoke. Sana Moreau went last, as the fastest of all.

The machine took four samples at a time. Hale loaded it with a technician's care and a sceptic's face while Illuminara stood behind the curtain and did not touch the controls. Four twelve-minute runs fit before 16:15, including the final run of two samples, and the room went quiet with a texture it had not had at the third fever.

In the fourth run the order broke. Osvin's grand-niece Ines, her left forearm splinted from the slide, sat on a stretcher beside his bed. She lived in a pale-stock house below the church. By Marta's list and Illuminara's ranking she belonged near the fast end. She stood fourth from the slow end.

**Corin Hale**  
There. One in fourteen. Your hearth explains thirteen and fumbles the other.

**Illuminara**  
It is wrong. Good. A hearth that explained all fourteen would be a story. Marta—where did Ines sit today?

**Marta Vell**  
She sat on that stretcher beside Osvin. They carried him here from the slide at nine, and she has not left his bed.
Illuminara did not move for a moment. She had been looking at the houses, and the smoke she had been looking for had been in the room she was standing in.

**Illuminara**  
Dr. Rusk. What does this clinic burn?

**Pelagia Rusk**

There was a silence in which the hum of the machine was the loudest thing in the building.

**Illuminara**  
Then the clinic is dosing every patient while they wait. The longer we argue, the slower the clearance. We are not waiting out the danger. We are feeding it.
On the screen the last pair settled. Sana Moreau, fastest of all, as written. The only fever in the room now was in Hale's face, and he was too honest a physician to hide that it was shame.

scenes.title: The Stove
paragraphs: *Nemea clinic, waiting room · 16:20 to 17:46*

The stove stood at the end of the room like a low black animal, and a dozen faces turned from it to her as she came in. It was nine degrees outside the blanket line. Eight patients lay in shock with their feet toward the heat.

**Pelagia Rusk**  
No. If that goes cold, I lose the spleen and the girl to the chill before any anaesthetic touches them. You have found a poison and want me to put out the only fire.

**Illuminara**

**Marta Vell**  
Forty cakes. It was to last the village until the thaw. I can put the bakery's hot soapstone under the two shock beds while the first grate catches, but the stones will not hold all night.

**Illuminara**  
Then I am asking you for the winter, and your stones buy the swap time. I will not pretend either is small.

**Pelagia Rusk**  
Temperatures every four minutes. If any bed loses half a degree before the pale side catches, the dark grate stays lit. That is my stop condition.

Marta did not answer for the time it takes to count forty cakes against a hundred houses. Behind her a man lying under a coat said something about his own hearth and what it had meant for four hundred years, and she said, without turning, that the hearth had meant it for the living.

**Marta Vell**  
Open the storehouse. But I want it written that the village gave it, and that the dark cake does not go to the lowlands to be sold. It goes in the river.

**Illuminara**  
Written, and I will sign it where the village can read it.

At 16:36 the girl's bedside reading had fallen four tenths of a degree. Rusk ordered the dark grate held for four more minutes; Marta shifted both hottest stones beneath the child and wrapped the exposed leg above the splint. **Nell Brandt, on the radio**  
The spleen and the girl's leg are the two your blocks cannot reach. I lift at seventeen with those two. The third stretcher space stays empty; nobody else is beyond the blocks, and I will not delay them to fill it. Note that I am not waiting for your assay.

**Illuminara**  
Do not wait. Carry them. The next readings are for the twelve who remain.

At 17:04, forty minutes after the swap began and two minutes after Brandt lifted, Hale drew the second plasma set. Twelve minutes later the slopes had begun to rise. They rose unevenly, and Osvin Pike, who had breathed the most, had risen almost not at all.

**Corin Hale**  
Told you. He is the one it is in the blood for.

**Illuminara**  
He is also the one who has sat longest in the smoke. Draw him again at 17:34, seventy minutes after the swap began. If I am wrong about him, I will be glad to learn it now.

**Corin Hale**

scenes.title: What the Pass Kept
paragraphs: *Nemea clinic and landing field · 17:00 to 04:10*

The helicopter lifted at 17:02 with the girl of nine and the man with the ruptured spleen, and went up into the beginning of the rain with its lights burning. Brandt radioed from the valley at 17:58 that they were down and handed over. The second lift at nineteen hundred stood on the pad unneeded, and she logged it that way, and told Illuminara afterwards that it was the best use of a flight she had ever made.

Dr. Hale blocked the eight urgent patients who remained. He worked from the least recovered to the most, with Rusk's hands beside his, and each time the plasma line had said who should be blocked and each time the family or the patient had said yes to the number. The four who had been stable enough to wait cleared his line in the early hours, went under the general and woke without fevers. The blocks took twice as long and held. Ines, her forearm dressed after her turn, fell asleep against the wall before Osvin Pike was wheeled in last at three-forty.
At 04:10 the last suture was in. In the waiting room the stove burned pale cake with its vents open, and nobody was cold, and nobody was feverish.

Illuminara stayed through the rest of the night because there was a log to finish. She wrote the protocol herself, in a plain hand, as Hale would use it and not as she would. A bench test: plasma and a clear substrate, with the oxygen sensor reading the consumption rate, twelve minutes, no drug given. A line below which a patient was blocked, not put under. A pair of readings half an hour apart for anyone who breathed smoke of unknown stock, because the slope moved and the machine could tell. Under it she wrote the name of the village that had given the winter, and the date, and Marta Vell signed it where the village could read it.

**Pelagia Rusk**  
What does it cost us? Say the whole of it.

**Illuminara**  
Forty cakes of pale resin, which is the village's heat until the thaw. Dark cake does not burn indoors in Nemea again, and the kilns stand idle until someone finds what in the scorched bark does this. Two of the fourteen face long recoveries far from home. **Pelagia Rusk**  
Checked. But it was right tonight.

**Illuminara**  
It was wrong once tonight, about Osvin's niece, and that is why it was right about the stove.

Rusk looked down the ward, where the patients slept in the pale light of the new fire. Then she asked Marta Vell to bring in forty cakes from the cold storehouse, and Marta, who had been awake for twenty-two hours, said she would bring them herself.

story.title: THE VILLAGE THAT COULD NOT SLEEP
story.deck: Fourteen wounded villagers need surgery before the pass closes, every anaesthetic the clinic owns brings the same fever, and the one thing the patients share is not in their blood.
story.shape: Intimate medical emergency in five scenes: a pattern read from the order of the reactions, a prediction written down before the test, one miss that exposes the real source in the clinic itself, and a costly village-wide agreement; the physician, the pilot, the headwoman and the anaesthetist each keep a veto.

scenes.title: Fever
